title: [bug] spec check reports 'passed' for a document it could not parse
description:
A document whose frontmatter parses as YAML but does not decode into the document envelope is indexed with a parse_error and no frontmatter (AC-SPEC-002.4, working as specified). corpus.Corpus.check then skips it — 'if entry.Frontmatter == nil { continue }', cli/core/corpus/check.go — and the run reports every rule as outcome 'passed' with zero findings.

Reproduced 2026-08-05 on this branch. A probe at specs/adrs/ADR-999-probe.md declaring 'status: totally-made-up' AND 'slug: adr-001' (already held by ADR-001):

  $ spec check specs/adrs/ADR-999-probe.md
  no findings
  checks:
    frontmatter/missing-property  passed
    frontmatter/schema            passed
    slug/duplicate                passed
    slug/pattern-mismatch         passed
  $ echo $?
  0

Two separate error-severity defects, reported as four passes. Not a stale-index artifact: it reproduces with specs/specs.json deleted first. 'spec index --out -' records the entry correctly, with the message and span — so the CLI HAS the fact and the checker declines to report it.

This inverts the FRD's own division of labour. REQ-SPEC-002's rationale is that the indexer exits zero on parse failures because 'a build failure is the checker's job, not the indexer's'. The checker does not do that job, so nothing does: the worst-formed document in a corpus is the one document 'spec check --strict' is guaranteed to be silent about, and it reports that silence as a pass.

The check.go doc comment states the current behaviour deliberately ('has already been reported through ... the member's own parse_error and is not revisited here'). That reasoning holds for an EXCLUSION — a file with no frontmatter is not a spec document. It does not hold for a parse error: that document declared itself a spec document and got the declaration wrong. And 'already reported' means reported in the index, an artifact 'spec check' never shows the caller.

SPEC GAP, not just a code bug. No AC covers it: AC-SPEC-002.4/002.5 govern the indexer, and REQ-SPEC-003's ACs all presuppose parsed frontmatter. Adding an AC to REQ-SPEC-003 is part of this work — approximately: 'WHEN a corpus member is indexed with a parse error, the CLI SHALL report a finding carrying that error's message and span, and SHALL NOT report any check as passed for that document.'

Design (worked out, not guessed):
  1. schemas/finding.strata — add a FindingFrontmatterParse variant to the
     FindingDetail union, carrying the parse error's message. The union's
     own doc comment already sanctions this: 'a later check adds a variant
     without changing the envelope that carries it'. Regenerate via
     scripts/generate-schemas.sh (needs strata).
  2. cli/core/finding — add RuleFrontmatterParse = 'frontmatter/parse' and
     a FrontmatterParse(path, at, message) constructor, matching the
     existing four.
  3. cli/core/corpus/check.go — in the entry.Frontmatter == nil branch,
     emit that finding when entry.ParseError != nil rather than
     'continue'. Correct the doc comment, which currently records the
     wrong behaviour as intended.
  4. cli/cmd/check.go — add the rule to checkRules so it is accounted for
     in the report and reachable via --only.
  5. Tests: a corpus fixture with an undecodable document asserting one
     finding rather than zero; a cmd-level snapshot case. Note that
     cli/profile/self_application_test.go would NOT have caught this — it
     asserts exclusions == 1 and findings == 0, and a parse-error entry is
     neither an exclusion nor a finding.

INTERIM MITIGATION IN PLACE: .github/workflows/checks.yml's corpus job
has a 'No document failed to parse' step that greps the emitted index for
parse_error entries. Delete that step when this lands — it exists only
because the check is silent.
acceptance_criteria: spec check reports an error-severity finding for a document indexed with a parse_error, and does not report any rule as passed for that document; exit status is non-zero; REQ-SPEC-003 carries an AC covering it; the interim workflow step in checks.yml is removed
notes:
REAL-WORLD TRIGGER (2026-08-05): the framework's own templates, via the authoring workflow the spec skill prescribes.

SKILL.md step 1 says copy a template from references/ as the starting point. Every template ships 'updated_at: <YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ>' as a placeholder. SKILL.md step 7 says run 'spec check <path>'. Between those two steps — i.e. for the entire authoring session, which is exactly when an agent checks its work — the document carries a placeholder that fails RFC 3339 parsing, so the envelope decode fails and every check reports passed.

Reproduced by copying adr-template.md, filling in title/description/slug, and leaving updated_at as the template left it:

  $ spec check specs/adrs/ADR-018-caching-layer.md
  no findings
  checks:
    frontmatter/missing-property  passed
    frontmatter/schema            passed
    slug/duplicate                passed
    slug/pattern-mismatch         passed
  $ echo $?
  0

Note that updated_at is a REQUIRED property and frontmatter/missing-property also reports passed. The check that exists for this property is silent about it.

Also confirmed on a real committed file: plugin/skills/spec/references/work-order-template.md (bead 6n4, 'mapping value is not allowed in this context') indexes with a parse_error, and 'spec check --strict' over a corpus containing it exits 0.

SEVERITY IS INVERTED. Three realistic defects, same corpus:
  version: 1.2 (unquoted, YAML float)  -> REPORTED (frontmatter/schema)
  status: proposed (Nygard's classic)  -> SILENT
  updated_at: 2026-07-29 (date only)   -> SILENT
A typo in a value that still decodes is caught; a value that breaks the envelope is not. The worse the defect, the quieter the tool.

The third case is AC-SPEC-003.2's OWN worked example, verbatim: 'updated_at: 2026-07-29 fails an RFC 3339 date-time check, even though a YAML parser would coerce it to a valid timestamp before any check could see it.' Strictly the AC's WHEN-trigger arguably never fires, since the CLI never reaches validation — but the example the FRD chose to demonstrate the requirement with produces no finding at all. Whatever the lawyering, REQ-SPEC-003 illustrates itself with a case the implementation does not handle, which is strong evidence the intent is unmet rather than merely unspecified.

Scanned all 66 commits of history: zero instances of an envelope-breaking status or updated_at in committed docs/ or specs/ documents. The corpus has been careful, not protected — every document that would have triggered this was authored correctly by hand.
close_reason: spec check now reports frontmatter/parse at severity error for any member indexed with a parse error; AC-SPEC-003.6 added to REQ-SPEC-003; corpus regression tests plus the check-frontmatter-parse snapshot case; interim workflow step removed

title: specs.toml points [workspace].root at docs/, so the CLI indexes an empty corpus
description:
Found by orchestrator smoke-test of the binary built from bge.12, run from
the repository root:

    $ spec index --out -
    { "workspace": "agent-plugins", "entries": [], "exclusions": [
        { "path": "docs/session-bootstrap.md", "reason": "no-frontmatter" } ] }

    $ spec check
    no findings
    checks: frontmatter/schema passed, slug/duplicate passed, ...
    exit=0

`specs.toml` declares `[workspace].root = "docs"`. `docs/` holds exactly one
markdown file and no specification documents; the corpus is the 27 documents
under `specs/`. So every command answers over an EMPTY corpus:

- `check` reports "no findings" and exits 0 — a clean bill of health on
  nothing. This is the vacuous-pass failure mode, reproduced in the shipped
  product: identical in kind to `scripts/validate-corpus.py` searching
  `docs/` (`rfcs/inbox/feature-blueprint/rfc-0010` P1) and to the Definition
  of Done's `docs/` anchor, both already corrected.
- `slug-exists frd-spec-validation-cli` answers "not found" for a slug that
  exists.
- `next-id adr` answers 1 with sixteen ADRs in the corpus.

This is NOT a new decision: the corpus root was confirmed as `specs/` by the
author on 2026-08-04, recorded on agent-plugins-bge.14. `specs.toml` is the
one place that was never updated — it predates the reorg (last touched in
bb8ef2a).

Implemented in the orchestrator's own loop rather than delegated: it is a
one-line configuration correction applying an already-recorded decision.

## Retro

**Approach.** One line: `specs.toml` `[workspace].root` from `docs` to
`specs`. Implemented in the orchestrator loop rather than delegated — it
applies a decision the author already recorded on bge.14 (the corpus root
is `specs/`), so there was nothing to decide, and dispatching an agent for
one TOML line would cost more than it saves.

**How it was found — not by a test.** By smoke-testing the binary built
from bge.12 against the real repository. Every gate in this run was green
while the shipped CLI answered over an empty corpus. The unit and
integration suites each construct their own fixture roots, and bge.14's
self-application gate resolves `specs/` from the test file's own path, so
nothing in the suite ever reads the committed `[workspace].root`. That is
the real gap: no test asserts that the shipped configuration points at the
actual corpus.

**Verified after the change**, from the repository root:

- `index --out -` gives 26 entries, 1 exclusion (was 0 entries)
- `slug-exists frd-spec-validation-cli` resolves to
  `specs/features/spec-index/spec-index-frd.md` (was "not found")
- `next-id adr` gives 17 (was 1)
- `check` reports one finding — the known `/plan` additionalProperties
  violation at `spec-index-blueprint.md:12:7` — and exits 1 (was "no
  findings", exit 0)

That last line is the point: exit status now reflects a real defect instead
of an empty corpus, which is AC-SPEC-006.6 and AC-SPEC-006.9 doing their
job against real data for the first time.

**Implicit decision.** `docs/session-bootstrap.md` is left out of the
corpus; it is not a specification document and correctly falls outside the
new root.

**Fourth instance of one root cause.** The `specs/` reorg left `docs/`
references behind in `scripts/validate-corpus.py` (rfc-0010 P1), the
blueprint's Definition of Done, the blueprint's Tracker Reconciliation
(agent-plugins-mvx), and now `specs.toml`. Each was found by a different
mechanism and none by the others — a sweep for any remaining is warranted.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] `specs.toml` declares `[workspace].root = "specs"`.
- [ ] `spec index --out -` emits entries for the corpus (27 documents), not an empty list.
- [ ] `spec slug-exists frd-spec-validation-cli` reports found, with its path.
- [ ] `spec next-id adr` returns one greater than the highest ADR in use.
- [ ] `cd cli && go test ./...` still passes, including the bge.14 self-application gate.
- [ ] `spec check` exit status reflects real findings rather than an empty corpus.

metadata.tier_reason: Implemented in the orchestrator loop; one-line config fix applying a recorded decision, but it changes what every command sees so the gates must be re-run.

title: Split findings from the close artifact: retro: comments own findings, the file becomes handoff.md, and bb-close-bead.sh stops rewriting the description
description:
The per-bead artifact records findings in three places, and two of them are
redundant.

Measured on the committed ledger 2026-08-10:

- The subagent writes `{ID}.retro.md` — the bead description plus a
  `## Retro — implementation` section.
- `bb-close-bead.sh` closes with `bd update --status closed --body-file
  <that file>`, and `--body-file` **replaces** the description. So the retro
  lands inside the bead description.
- The same findings are ALSO written as `retro:`-prefixed `bd comment`s.

Cost of the description copy: across 44 closed beads, retro prose inside
descriptions totals **~269 KB of a 968 KB `.beads/issues.jsonl` — 28% of the
whole tracker file** — and `bd export` rewrites the entire file on every close.
Per-bead examples: `9kb.10` 20,989 of 22,743 description bytes are retro;
`bge.13` 17,568 of 19,734.

It also destroys content. `34g` established the mechanism: agents hand-retype
the description into the retro file and drop parts of it, and `--body-file`
writes the lossy copy back. Verified on `agent-plugins-9kb.1` — the original
description (from `git show f019922^:.beads/issues.jsonl`) ended with a
`## Retro` section carrying the findings-capture instruction; the current
description has the heading and neither the instruction nor the reference.

**Decisions taken 2026-08-10, after working through the alternatives:**

1. **`bb-close-bead.sh` stops writing the description.** Closing a bead must not
   rewrite its groomed content.
2. **`retro:` bd comments remain the findings channel.** They are the shared
   protocol across `retro-spec`, `groom-feature-blueprint` and
   `work-order-template.md`; bead-bonanza will not deviate from it. Harmonizing
   process across skills is worth more than a local optimization. Measured:
   comments DO survive — `bd export` carries a `comments` array on the issue
   record, and 40 issue-lines in the committed ledger already hold `retro:`
   payload across 33 beads.
3. **The file stops carrying findings** and becomes a bare handoff artifact,
   renamed to remove the word "retro" — it is no longer a retrospective and the
   name misleads.
design:
Three coordinated changes. They touch the same call site in three prompt
templates, so they are one bead, not three.

## 1. Rename the artifact and reduce it

`{RUN_DIR}/{ID}.retro.md` becomes `{RUN_DIR}/{ID}.handoff.md`. It is a handoff
from whoever worked the bead to whoever finishes it — correct whether the
subagent completed normally or died mid-ceremony.

**Its content is narrower than the old file by a lot.** The phase reached is
already in `{ID}.progress.jsonl`; do not restate it, or the two sources drift
and `references/recovery.md`'s "the ledger is a hint, never the authority" rule
has two hints to reconcile. The handoff carries only what the close needs and
nothing else can supply:

- **The paths to stage.** The orchestrator cannot infer these from
  `git status` in a shared tree — that is the foreign-dirt problem the pathspec
  guard exists for.
- **Any close-specific caveat** — a prior `WIP <bead-id>` commit that must be
  squashed first, a regen step that must run before staging, a fixture the bead
  regenerated.

Typically four lines. Write the template that way; do not leave room for prose.

## 2. `bb-close-bead.sh` drops the body file

Current interface:

```
bb-close-bead.sh <bead-id> <priority> <title> <retro-file> [path ...]
```

New:

```
bb-close-bead.sh <bead-id> <priority> <title> [path ...]
```

The script closes with a plain `bd update --status closed` and leaves the
description exactly as grooming wrote it. The handoff file stops being an input
to the script; it is an artifact the orchestrator's acceptance check verifies.

- Remove the "refuses to run without a retro file" guard and replace it with
  nothing — the acceptance check owns that now.
- Update the script's own header usage line AND the interface published in
  `SKILL.md`. The skill states the script is authoritative on disagreement, so
  both must move in this commit.
- This is a **breaking change to a script three prompt templates call.** Update
  the per-bead, doc/chore fast-lane and shared-surface batch templates in
  `references/subagent-prompts.md` in the same commit, plus the replay
  invocation in `references/recovery.md`.

## 3. The template's step 5 keeps findings, in comments only

Rewrite step 5 of the per-bead template so the findings trigger list produces
**`retro:` comments only** — one `bd comment` per finding on `{ID}` — and the
handoff file carries no findings at all. Keep the trigger list itself verbatim
(it is what `34g` established, and it filters where a category list enumerates);
keep "a clean bead records none — say so rather than inventing filler".

The three items that were file-only — what you tried that did not work, what you
decided silently, the observed pre-fix failure on a defect bead — become
comments too, each its own `retro:` comment. They are findings; the file was
only ever their container.

## Sweep

`grep -rn "retro.md\|retro-file\|body-file" plugin/skills/bead-bonanza/` and
resolve every hit. Known: `SKILL.md`'s recovery pointer and script interface
table, `references/recovery.md`'s crash-resilient-close section and its replay
command, all three templates, and `scripts/bb-close-bead.sh`. The acceptance
check in the sibling Phase 3 bead also names the file — coordinate rather than
leaving one of the two wrong.

Do NOT change `bb-progress.sh`, `bb-verify-skip.sh`, the phase vocabulary, or
the close ceremony's ordering constraints.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] bb-close-bead.sh no longer accepts or uses a body file, and closes with a plain 'bd update --status closed'
- [ ] A closed bead's description is byte-identical to its pre-close description
- [ ] The script's header usage line and the interface published in SKILL.md both show the new four-argument form
- [ ] The per-bead, fast-lane and shared-surface templates and recovery.md's replay command all call the new form
- [ ] {ID}.retro.md is renamed {ID}.handoff.md everywhere, and 'grep -rn "retro.md" plugin/skills/bead-bonanza/' returns no stale reference
- [ ] The handoff template asks only for the paths to stage and any close-specific caveat, and does not restate the phase
- [ ] Step 5 produces findings as retro: comments only; the handoff file carries no findings
- [ ] The trigger list and the 'a clean bead records none' instruction survive verbatim
- [ ] The three former file-only items each become their own retro: comment
- [ ] bb-progress.sh, bb-verify-skip.sh, the phase vocabulary and the close ordering are unchanged

metadata.tier_reason: A breaking interface change to a script three templates call, plus a rename with a full reference sweep. A missed call site fails at close time, mid-run, on a bead that has already done its work.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: The per-bead template is itself inside a fenced code block, so the obvious way to specify the new handoff file — a literal fenced example of its contents — silently terminates the template's own fence. I wrote it that way first, saw the fence count go odd, and rewrote it as a two-item bullet list. Any bead that adds an example to a prompt template hits this.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: Settled without guidance: what a recovering orchestrator does when the handoff file is missing. The old text said 'reconstruct the close body from the description'; with no body file there is nothing to reconstruct, so recovery.md now says derive the paths from git status --porcelain and be strict about foreign dirt. The bead specified the removal but not the replacement.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: The bead scoped the reference sweep to plugin/skills/bead-bonanza/, but '.retro.md' also lives in scripts/check-skills.sh's IGNORE list of filenames-a-skill-describes. It is inert today (no backticked occurrence matches the checker's regex, before or after), and I renamed it to '.handoff.md' so the convention stays coherent rather than leaving a dangling entry.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: Silent choice a diff-reader would not see as a choice: the design said 'rewrite step 5', and I split it into step 5 (handoff file) and step 6 (retro: comments), renumbering the template's steps 6-9 to 7-10. Keeping both in one step would have re-coupled the two artifacts this bead exists to separate.

title: Add a sprint retro to Phase 4: synthesize the run's own evidence into how the next sprint runs better
description:
A bead-bonanza run is a sprint, and it has no retrospective.

What exists today stops at the per-bead level. Each subagent writes a
`.retro.md` about its own bead. Phase 4 prints a table, totals, an implicit-
decisions list, a tier-escalation table and a follow-up-beads list. Then
`SKILL.md:862-869` offers to run `retro-skill` on `bead-bonanza` — but only
"WHEN a run struggled", only about the skill itself, and never unprompted.

Nothing asks the question the run is best placed to answer: **how do we run the
next sprint more effectively?** Specifically —

- **Were the beads groomed well?** The run is the only place grooming's
  predictions get tested. Tier assignments meet reality here; so do
  acceptance criteria that turned out unsatisfiable, descriptions that failed
  the fresh-agent test in practice, and dependency edges that were wrong or
  missing.
- **Were the specs right?** Subagents hit spec gaps constantly — a blueprint
  that contradicted the repo, an AC that could not be met as declared, a
  contract that did not say what the implementer needed.
- **Was the plan right?** The amendments log now records every resequencing,
  reclassification and bounce. That log is a direct measurement of how good the
  original bucketing was, and nothing reads it.
- **Did the skill mislead?** Already covered by `retro-skill`, but currently
  triggered by vibe ("WHEN a run struggled") rather than by evidence the run
  collected.

Every input already exists or is being created: the amendments log, the
tier-escalation and over-routing tables, the ceremony-incomplete list, the
bounced-bead list, the mid-run admissions, and the harvested `retro:` comments
(53 of them in the one run where they were counted). They are produced, reported
individually, and never synthesized.

Origin: this bead was not proposed by any RFC. It came out of a review session
on 2026-08-10 whose framing was that a run is a sprint — and that a sprint
without a retrospective does not compound.
design:
Add a Phase 4 step, after the report and before the run-directory cleanup:
**the sprint retro**. Specify it in `references/final-report.md` alongside the
report specification, with the trigger and the routing in `SKILL.md`.

## When it runs

Every run that closed at least one bead. Not conditional on the run having
"struggled" — a clean run's evidence is exactly what calibrates against
over-caution, and the observed asymmetry (escalations expose under-routing while
over-routing succeeds silently) means a smooth run is the one most likely to be
hiding waste.

## Inputs — all already produced

| Input | Answers |
|---|---|
| `## Amendments` in `dispatch.md` | was the plan right? |
| Tier escalations + deliberate over-routes | was the routing calibrated? |
| Ceremony-incomplete / reconstructed beads | did the ceremony hold? |
| Bounced beads + their gaps | was the backlog groomed? |
| Mid-run admissions (in-scope vs filed-and-left) | was scope drawn correctly? |
| Harvested `retro:` comments | were the beads and specs right? |

The harvest must return non-zero before this step runs — a sprint retro over an
empty finding set is the confident-and-wrong artifact the harvest bead exists to
prevent. Assert, then aggregate.

## Output — four questions, then routing

Structure it as the four questions rather than as a narrative, so a reader can
see which are unanswered:

1. **Grooming** — which beads were under-groomed, and how did that show up?
   Which tier predictions were wrong in which direction?
2. **Specs** — which spec documents did an implementer find wrong, thin or
   contradictory?
3. **Plan** — what did the amendments log record, and what would have produced a
   better initial bucketing?
4. **Skill** — where did `bead-bonanza` itself mislead, and what was improvised
   around?

Then route, rather than pooling everything into one artifact — this is where the
existing skills already own the downstream work:

- Grooming and tier findings -> `groom-beads`' retro loop, which explicitly
  consumes escalation evidence to recalibrate its routing rubric.
- Spec findings -> `retro-spec`, which produces improvement RFCs against the
  project's own documents.
- Skill findings -> `retro-skill`, which produces an RFC against
  `bead-bonanza`. Replace the current vibe trigger at `SKILL.md:862-869` with
  this: the sprint retro decides whether there is enough evidence for a skill
  RFC, and says so either way.

Each route is an *offer*, not an automatic dispatch — the run has just finished
and the user may not want three more agents. Present the four answers, name
which routes have material, and let the user pick. State explicitly when a
question has no findings; a null result is a result, and "grooming: no findings
across 12 beads" is worth more than silence.

## Keep it cheap

The sprint retro is a synthesis of artifacts that already exist, not a fresh
investigation. It reads the run directory and the harvested comments; it does not
re-read the diff or re-derive the run. If it is expensive it will be skipped, and
a skipped retro is the default state this bead exists to change.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Phase 4's sprint retro runs after the report and before the run-directory cleanup, on every run that closed at least one bead
- [ ] It harvests retro: comments via the bd export | jq pipeline and asserts a non-zero count before aggregating
- [ ] It writes one report per run at rfcs/sprints/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<epic-slug>.md
- [ ] The report carries every harvested finding verbatim, including those that warrant no RFC, and states why the tail is kept
- [ ] The report answers the four questions — grooming, specs, plan, skill — and states a null result explicitly rather than omitting a question
- [ ] RFCs are written to rfcs/inbox/<skill>/ and cite the report rather than re-inlining its evidence
- [ ] One row per sprint is appended to rfcs/retro-log.md
- [ ] Findings are routed to groom-beads, retro-spec and retro-skill as offers the user accepts or declines
- [ ] The vibe-triggered 'Retro this skill' section is replaced by the sprint retro's skill question
- [ ] The step reads comments and the run's own tables; it does not re-read diffs or re-derive the run
notes:
## Output shape decided 2026-08-10

Three artifacts, distinct jobs, all produced before the run directory is deleted.

1. **One sprint report per run** at `rfcs/sprints/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<epic-slug>.md`
   — e.g. `2026-08-10-harden-bead-bonanza.md`. Dated and slugged rather than
   keyed on the run id, because `1786345424-bbh` means nothing to a human
   scanning the directory. It lives under `rfcs/` because that is where the
   retro apparatus already lives (`retro-log.md`, `inbox/`, `outbox/`,
   `retired/`); keeping them together is deliberate harmonization, not filing
   convenience.

   The report carries **every finding verbatim, including the below-threshold
   tail**, plus the four questions answered. This is load-bearing:
   `triage-rfc`'s deferral model runs on recurrence, so a finding that appears
   once and is not written down can never be observed appearing twice. Filtering
   to RFC-worthy findings only would silently break the accumulation model.

2. **RFCs** into `rfcs/inbox/<skill>/` for findings that clear the bar. They
   **cite** the report rather than re-inlining it, so report and RFC cannot
   disagree: the report is the testimony, the RFC is the proposal built on it.

3. **A row in `rfcs/retro-log.md`** so one index covers all retro activity,
   the same way RFC ingestion is logged today.

**Harvest from comments, not from files.** The findings channel is
`retro:`-prefixed `bd comment`s (shared protocol, confirmed 2026-08-10); the
per-bead file is now a bare `handoff.md` carrying no findings. Use the
corrected `bd export | jq` pipeline from the sibling harvest bead — NOT
text-parsing of `bd show`, and NOT reading the run directory.

metadata.tier_reason: Designs a new phase step and its routing across three sibling skills, deciding what a run can conclude about its own grooming, specs and plan.

title: The prescribed findings harvest returns zero on a completed run: bd list hides closed beads and bd show --json hides comments
description:
`SKILL.md:797-802` wires findings capture — "record `retro:`-prefixed
`bd comment`s on the bead being worked" — and hands aggregation to "the
feature's final DoD bead". It names no harvest command. The vendored protocol
(`rfcs/findings-capture.md`, Aggregation) supplies the only one:
"`bd list --label <feature-slug>` then each issue's `retro:` comments."

**Both halves fail silently on a completed run.** Measured:

```
$ bd list --label feature-spec-validation-cli --json | len                 -> 16
$ bd list --label feature-spec-validation-cli --status closed --json | len -> 20
$ bd show agent-plugins-bge.8 --json  | jq '.comments | length'            -> 0
$ bd show agent-plugins-bge.8 | grep -cE '^\s+retro:'                      -> 7
```

`bd list` defaults to open issues, and a drained closure set is almost entirely
closed. `bd show --json` omits comments entirely while the text output prints
them. Following the protocol as written yields **0 findings where 53 across 15
beads exist.** The orchestrator reported zero to the user before catching it.

The failure runs in the worst direction: an aggregated retro over an empty set
produces a confident, clean-looking artifact. And it is already known —
`retro-skill/SKILL.md`'s own script-defect *example* cites the `bd list` half
("returns ~nothing at aggregation time because it defaults to open issues"). It
is illustrated in one skill and still unfixed in the protocol every project
vendors.

Evidence that the fix works: the final DoD bead in that run received the
corrected mechanism in its dispatch prompt and harvested exactly 53 findings,
matching the independently counted total.

This blocks the sprint-retro bead, which has nothing to aggregate until the
harvest returns what exists.


## Steps to Reproduce

Against any feature whose beads are largely closed and carry `retro:` comments:

```
$ bd list --label <feature-slug> --json | jq length
16                                   # open only — most of the set is missing
$ bd list --label <feature-slug> --status closed --json | jq length
20                                   # the rest
$ bd show <a-closed-bead> --json | jq '.comments | length'
0                                    # comments omitted from JSON
$ bd show <a-closed-bead> | grep -cE '^\s+retro:'
7                                    # they are in the text output
```

**Expected:** the protocol's harvest (`bd list --label <slug>`, then each
issue's `retro:` comments via `bd show --json`) returns every finding.
**Actual:** it returns 0 where 53 across 15 beads exist, and reports cleanly.
design:
**1. State the harvest in `bead-bonanza` rather than delegating it.** In the
findings-capture principle (moving to `references/operating-principles.md`):

> Harvest with `bd list --label <slug> --status closed` **and** the default open
> query — a drained closure set is mostly closed, and `bd list` shows open
> issues only. (WHERE the installed `bd` has `--all`, prefer it; note that
> repeating `--status` overwrites rather than accumulates.) Read comments from
> `bd show <id>` **TEXT** output: `--json` omits them. Assert the count is
> non-zero before aggregating; a harvest returning zero findings across a
> completed feature is a broken query, not a clean run, and an aggregated retro
> built on it is worse than none.

The non-zero assertion is the load-bearing half. Make it an explicit step with a
stated failure action — stop and re-run the query, do not aggregate — rather
than advice.

**2. Fix the local vendored copy.** `rfcs/findings-capture.md`'s Aggregation
section carries the wrong command. Correct it, and note in the file that the
correction is pending upstream so it is not reverted by the next sync. Check
whether it is generated by a sync script before hand-editing — if it is, the
edit belongs upstream and the local copy is regenerated.

**3. Send the correction upstream.** The wrong command is published in
`findings-capture-protocol.md`, owned by `retro-spec`, and reaches every project
that vendors it. Write an RFC to `rfcs/outbox/` against `retro-spec` carrying:
the two measured causes, the four-command evidence block above, and the
corrected instruction. Follow the outbox's existing RFC conventions and the
`skill-rfc-template`. This is the half with reach — the local fix protects one
project, the upstream fix protects all of them.

**4. Own the channel in the dispatch templates.** `grep -c
"findings-capture\|retro:" references/subagent-prompts.md` returns **0** — the
`retro:` comment instruction reached subagents in the observed run only because
the groomed bead descriptions happened to carry it, which is why the three
prerequisite beads outside that groomed plan produced retro files and no
findings at all. Putting the obligation into the template is the retro-reshape
bead's territory; cross-reference it rather than doing it twice, but do not
close this bead believing the channel is wired if that one has not landed.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] The skill states the harvest as a single 'bd export | jq' pipeline over closed and open beads, not as text-parsing of bd show
- [ ] The stated command was run against a drained bead set and returned a non-zero count matching an independent count, with both figures in the retro
- [ ] A non-zero assertion is an explicit step with a stated failure action, not advice
- [ ] rfcs/findings-capture.md's Aggregation section carries the corrected command, or the correction was made at its generating source
- [ ] An RFC against retro-spec is written to rfcs/outbox/ carrying both measured causes and the bd export form
- [ ] The retro: comment obligation is retained everywhere it currently appears
notes:
## Corrected 2026-08-10 — the prescribed remedy was itself wrong

This bead's Design said to read comments from `bd show <id>` TEXT output
because `--json` omits them. Measured on bd 1.1.2:

    $ bd show agent-plugins-92q.9 --json | jq '.[0] | has("comments")'
    false
    $ bd export | jq 'select(.id=="agent-plugins-92q.9") | .comments | length'
    1

`bd show --json` omits comments, but **`bd export` carries them** as a
`comments` array on the issue record — 40 issue-lines in the committed ledger
already hold `retro:` payload across 33 beads. So the harvest is JSON-native
after all, and text-parsing `bd show` was an unnecessary and fragile remedy.

**Use this form instead of the one in the Design:**

    bd export | jq -r 'select(.status=="closed")
      | select((.labels//[]) | index("<slug>"))
      | .comments[]? | select(.text|startswith("retro:")) | .text'

One command, no status flag to forget (export carries every status), no text
parsing. The two failure causes the bead documents are both real; only the
prescribed fix changes.

**Scope confirmed 2026-08-10:** the `retro:` comment channel STAYS. It is the
shared protocol across retro-spec, groom-feature-blueprint and
work-order-template.md, and bead-bonanza will not deviate from it. The outbox
RFC to retro-spec still goes — their published harvest is genuinely broken —
and should carry this corrected command rather than the text-parsing one.

title: The close ceremony exports a shared database, so the orchestrator's pathspec guard cannot work — defer tracker writes while a claim is held
description:
The skill's guard against a bead commit absorbing another actor's work is aimed
at the git index, while the capture happens upstream of it.

`SKILL.md:787-796` states the guard:

> the orchestrator commits its own work by explicit pathspec
> (`git commit -- <files>`) so a concurrently-staged tracker ledger rides with
> the next bead commit instead of being swept up mid-ceremony.

But `scripts/bb-close-bead.sh:64-72` runs a full `bd export`, regenerating the
**entire** ledger from the Dolt database every agent in the tree shares, and
line 85 stages it unconditionally:

```sh
before=""; [ -f .beads/issues.jsonl ] && before="$(git hash-object .beads/issues.jsonl)"
if ! bd export > /tmp/bb-export.$$ 2>/dev/null; then
...
[ -f .beads/issues.jsonl ]      && git add .beads/issues.jsonl
```

So any tracker write the orchestrator makes while a subagent sits between
`claimed` and `committed` is *inside the export that subagent commits*,
regardless of what either party passes to `git add`. **No pathspec discipline on
either side can prevent it.**

Observed: while the `bge.12` subagent held the tree, the orchestrator baked a
decision into `agent-plugins-tff` and wired two dependency edges — all
tracker-only writes, no files touched. It then ran
`git commit -- .beads/issues.jsonl .beads/interactions.jsonl` exactly as the
guard prescribes and got `nothing to commit, working tree clean`, because
`bb-close-bead.sh` had already exported and committed those edits inside
`39e0e6a agent-plugins-bge.12 P1 Build the four-subcommand command tree`.
Confirmed by reading the committed ledger:
`git show 39e0e6a:.beads/issues.jsonl` contains tff's `DECISION (2026-08-05)`
section.

Nothing was lost, but "One commit per bead, always" silently did not hold — that
commit carries another actor's work.

A `git status` check before the orchestrator commits does not fix this and was
considered and rejected: the run *did* check, and the window between the check
and the commit is exactly where the close ceremony landed. Ordering discipline
cannot close a race on shared state.


## Steps to Reproduce

1. Dispatch a subagent for a bead and let it reach `claimed` — it now holds the
   tree between `claimed` and `committed`.
2. From the orchestrator, make any tracker-only write: `bd update <other-id>`
   to bake a decision, or `bd dep add` to wire an edge. Touch no files.
3. Let the subagent's close ceremony run to completion.
4. From the orchestrator, commit its own work exactly as the guard prescribes:
   `git commit -- .beads/issues.jsonl .beads/interactions.jsonl`

**Expected:** the orchestrator's tracker edits land in their own commit.
**Actual:** `nothing to commit, working tree clean` — `bb-close-bead.sh`'s
`bd export` had already regenerated the full ledger, and the subagent's commit
carries the orchestrator's edits. Confirm with
`git show <bead-commit>:.beads/issues.jsonl` and grep for the other bead's
change. Observed as `39e0e6a` carrying `agent-plugins-tff`'s
`DECISION (2026-08-05)` section.
design:
**1. Replace the guard's second sentence** (`SKILL.md:789-792`, in the
"Guard against foreign dirt and index races" principle — which moves to
`references/operating-principles.md`; put the full text there and keep a
one-line rule above the cap):

> The tracker ledger is a projection of a database every agent shares, not a
> file one agent owns. `bb-close-bead.sh` regenerates it in full at each close,
> so any tracker write the orchestrator makes while a subagent is between
> `claimed` and `committed` lands in that subagent's commit — explicit pathspec
> cannot prevent this, because the capture happens before the index is
> consulted. WHILE any subagent holds a claim, the orchestrator SHALL confine
> itself to read-only `bd` queries and defer its own tracker writes — grooming a
> discovered bead, baking a decision, wiring an edge — until the wave returns.
> WHERE a write cannot wait, make it and note in the report which bead commit
> will carry it.

Keep the rest of the principle: the claim-reset rule (a subagent may only reset
a claim it made itself) and the pathspec rule are both still correct for the
cases they cover — foreign *working-tree* dirt is a different hazard from the
shared-database race, and the pathspec discipline remains the right defence
against it.

**2. Make a carried write visible.** Add to `bb-close-bead.sh` a line naming how
many issue records the export changed — on stdout, and in the commit message
body where a trailers file is in use. The script already hashes the ledger
before and after (`before="$(git hash-object .beads/issues.jsonl)"`), so it has
the comparison; what it lacks is a count and a report. A close that carried
foreign edits then shows up in review instead of being silent.

Suggested shape, cheap and dependency-free: diff the record ids present in the
old and new exports and report `export: N records changed (this bead: <id>)`,
so a count greater than one is the signal.

**3. Note the trade in the deferral rule itself.** Deferring orchestrator writes
can make a wave marginally slower when a discovered bead needs grooming
mid-flight. That is the intended trade and the WHERE clause is the escape hatch;
say so, or the next reader will treat the rule as unconditional and stall a wave
on it.

Interaction: the mid-run admission path (Phase 1.5 step 4) has the orchestrator
groom and wire edges for admitted beads — which is exactly a tracker write. The
deferral rule makes those wait for the wave boundary. Confirm that step's text
does not contradict this bead, and adjust it if it does.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] The guard states that the ledger is a projection of a shared database and that pathspec cannot prevent the capture
- [ ] The orchestrator is required to confine itself to read-only bd queries while any subagent holds a claim, with a stated escape hatch requiring the carrying commit to be reported
- [ ] The claim-reset rule and the working-tree pathspec rule are retained
- [ ] bb-close-bead.sh reports how many issue records the export changed, and a count above one is identified as the foreign-write signal
- [ ] The latency trade-off of deferral is stated alongside the rule
- [ ] Phase 1.5 step 4's mid-run admission text is consistent with the deferral rule
- [ ] The 'git status before committing' alternative is recorded as considered and rejected, with the reason

metadata.tier_reason: Replaces a guard with a timing rule and adds an export-delta report; must not weaken the two adjacent rules that are still correct.

title: bb-backup-run.sh: commit a self-describing run-directory snapshot each bead, and make the live directory authoritative
description:
The run directory holds everything a recovery needs and nothing keeps it alive.

**It dies with the container.** `SKILL.md:103` roots it at `${TMPDIR:-/tmp}`.
This project's `CLAUDE.md` states the container "is reclaimed after a period of
inactivity (or when the session ends)". Run `1786121603-ri`'s directory held
seven retro files of 4.3–17.5 KB — the documented input to the end-of-sprint
aggregated retro, and the run's only per-bead analysis — and the run had already
idled 2h16m, well into reclaim territory, with them unbacked.

**And the copy that was eventually taken lies by omission.**
`.bonanza/1786121603-ri/` was committed at 21:56 (`02c3cc8`, 17 paths) under the
same run id as the live directory. The live directory now holds five files the
backup does not: `agent-plugins-9kb.8.{progress.jsonl,retro.md,show.txt}` and
`agent-plugins-9kb.9.{progress.jsonl,retro.md}`, from beads that landed at 22:17
and 22:24 — after the snapshot. Nothing in the backup says it is partial or when
it was taken.

A retro run at 22:30 read the backup, found no `9kb.8`/`9kb.9` artifacts, and
reported both beads as having closed with no ceremony — then asserted that
`agent-plugins-9kb.9.progress.jsonl` "has never existed in this run directory".
It exists, with a complete seven-event trail ending
`{"phase":"committed","sha":"7761db5"}` and `{"phase":"pushed"}`. Both errors
trace to a backup that shares its name with the live directory and declares no
as-of time. **A stale twin under an identical name is worse than no backup,
because it answers confidently and wrongly.**

There is no `.bonanza/` directory in the tree today, so this is being built
fresh rather than repaired.
design:
Add `plugin/skills/bead-bonanza/scripts/bb-backup-run.sh` and the rules that
govern reading its output.

## The script

```
bb-backup-run.sh <run-dir> <dest>
```

Copies the run directory to `<dest>` and writes `SNAPSHOT.md` beside the copy
recording: the as-of timestamp, the source path, the run id, and the bead ids
whose `.retro.md` and `.progress.jsonl` are present. Idempotent — it is re-run
many times per run. bash 3.2 / BSD-safe like the others. Publish its usage line
in SKILL.md's script interface table.

## The rules

**Refresh after every bead's acceptance check**, not once per run. A copy taken
mid-run and never refreshed is indistinguishable from a complete one; this run's
went stale within 30 minutes. Hook it to the acceptance-check step so the two
cannot drift.

**The live run directory is authoritative; a snapshot never is.**

> Any procedure that reads the backup — recovery, a retro, a DoD audit — first
> checks whether the live directory still exists and uses it when it does. Read
> the backup only WHEN `$RUN_DIR` is gone, and then state the snapshot's as-of
> time in whatever you conclude from it.

Put this rule in `references/recovery.md` as well as in the backup section — it
is a reading rule, and recovery is where it will be needed.

**Commit it, do not gitignore it.** `.bonanza/<run-id>/` is committed while the
run is live. A gitignored copy lives in the working tree, which is reclaimed
with the container exactly like `/tmp` — it would move the artifacts without
making them durable. Only a pushed commit survives reclaim. Cost is small: this
run's directory was 152 KB across 17 files.

Copy the whole directory, not a filtered subset. Progress files are a few
hundred bytes each and are what make a post-mortem mechanical; deciding which
retros "matter" is a judgment best not made while the evidence is being
discarded.

**Delete it as the final step of Phase 4.** After the final report and before
handoff: `git rm -r .bonanza/<run-id>/`, committed on its own. It must not reach
the PR that carries the run's actual work — PR #16's review says so directly
("The `.bonanza` directory should be cleaned up as a last step in the bonanza.
We don't want to merge these with our PRs"). A run that ends with the directory
still tracked has not finished. Deleting it loses nothing: the commits that
added it stay in the branch history, reachable with
`git log --diff-filter=A -- '.bonanza/<run-id>/'` and `git show`. State that
where the deletion is prescribed, or the next reader will think the deletion is
the loss.

**Do not add `.bonanza/` to `.gitignore`.** Ignoring it and committing it are
mutually exclusive, and ignoring it silently removes the durability this exists
to provide. Consider a note in `.gitignore` saying so, so nobody adds it later
as a tidy-up.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] plugin/skills/bead-bonanza/scripts/bb-backup-run.sh exists, is idempotent, runs clean under 'bash -n', and uses no bash-4 or GNU-only constructs
- [ ] It writes SNAPSHOT.md recording as-of timestamp, source path, run id, and the bead ids whose handoff and progress files are present
- [ ] SNAPSHOT.md states that findings live in retro: bd comments and are not preserved by this directory
- [ ] Its usage line is published in SKILL.md's script interface table
- [ ] The skill requires a refresh after every bead's acceptance check, not once per run
- [ ] The 'live directory is authoritative, snapshot never is' rule appears in both the backup section and references/recovery.md
- [ ] The snapshot is committed under .bonanza/<run-id>/, with the reason a gitignored copy would not be durable stated
- [ ] Phase 4's deletion is gated on a committed sprint report and a non-zero harvest, and the gate is stated as a precondition rather than an ordering
- [ ] Deleting the directory is stated to lose nothing, with the git log command that reaches it afterwards
- [ ] .bonanza/ is not added to .gitignore
notes:
## Scope narrowed and a gate added, 2026-08-10

**The backup preserves operational state, not findings.** Findings now live in
`retro:` bd comments, which `bd export` carries into the committed
`.beads/issues.jsonl` — they are durable independently of this directory. The
per-bead file is a bare `handoff.md` (paths to stage, close caveats). So this
backup exists to make an interrupted run recoverable, and nothing in it is the
sole copy of anything a later reader needs. Say that in SNAPSHOT.md, so a
reader of a preserved directory knows what it is and is not.

**Add a deletion gate.** Phase 4's cleanup is currently ordered after the
report but not conditional on it. Make it conditional:

| The final `git rm -r .bonanza/<run-id>/` SHALL NOT run until the sprint
| report has been written and committed (`rfcs/sprints/<date>-<slug>.md`) and
| the harvest that fed it returned a non-zero count. A run that deletes its run
| directory without a committed report has destroyed its own evidence. Same
| shape as the per-bead acceptance check: the deletion is not permitted until
| the artifact that replaces it exists.

This is what makes the delete-at-Phase-4 rule safe rather than merely tidy.

metadata.tier_reason: Small script plus the reading rules that govern it; idempotency and BSD safety are the only subtleties and both are specified.

title: Phase 3: verify each bead's retro anchor and committed event exist before recording it closed
description:
Run `1786121603-ri` closed 12 beads. Nine carry a complete progress trail and a
retro anchor. Three — `9kb.5`, `9kb.6`, `9kb.7` — carry none, and the run
reached its final bead with nobody aware.

The live run directory holds a `.progress.jsonl` and a `.retro.md` for `tix`,
`ml9`, `j7f`, `9kb.1`–`9kb.4`, `9kb.8` and `9kb.9`. For `9kb.5` it holds a
two-event progress file and no retro; for `9kb.6` and `9kb.7`, nothing. All
three are closed in `bd` with landing commits `bb7ecc3`, `a43bcf9`, `da9d8bd`.
The epic's own progress note records the cause: "the previous three hand-written
briefs cost 9kb.5/.6/.7 their progress files and retro anchors".

The skill does forbid the proximate cause. `SKILL.md:625-627`: "Do not paraphrase
a template from memory". `SKILL.md:616-618` calls the retro file "the recovery
anchor, and it is non-negotiable". Both bind the *dispatch* step — and **no step
anywhere verifies the artifacts exist** before a bead is recorded closed or
before Phase 4 aggregates them. Three beads' worth of anchors went missing across
roughly three hours with no signal.

Adding emphasis to the existing warning is explicitly not the fix, for two
reasons. The skill already carries it. And it was not in the orchestrator's
context when the decision was made — it sits at line 625 of a file that
truncates at line 406 on re-injection after compaction. A warning that is absent
cannot be made louder. The fix is the check that catches the loss.
design:
Insert a step in Phase 3's post-return sequence, immediately after an outcome is
received and **before** the bead is written into the run table — alongside the
existing skip-claim verification, which is the same shape of check.

> **Acceptance check — every bead, every dispatch mode.** A bead is not closed
> until its artifacts exist:
>
> ```bash
> test -s "$RUN_DIR/$ID.retro.md" &&
>   grep -q '"phase":"committed"' "$RUN_DIR/$ID.progress.jsonl"
> ```
>
> On failure the bead's row is `ceremony-incomplete`, not `closed`. Reconstruct
> the missing retro from the subagent's returned summary and the bead's diff,
> append the missing events with `bb-progress.sh`, and record the reconstruction
> in the Phase 4 report. Do NOT reopen the bead or amend the commit — the work
> landed; only its record is missing.

Applies to batch subagents per bead, not per batch. A fast-lane subagent
processing six beads produces six pairs of artifacts, and the check runs six
times — that is precisely the case where a silent omission hides.

**Phase 4:** before the aggregated retro, list every bead whose anchor was
missing or reconstructed. An aggregated retro built from an incomplete anchor
set SHALL state which beads contributed nothing — otherwise it reads as a
complete picture of a run it only partly saw. (The Phase 4 report specification
moves to `references/final-report.md`; put it there and sequence accordingly.)

**Interaction with the sha-drift bead:** `grep -q '"phase":"committed"'` proves
an event was written, not that the sha in it is reachable. Where that sibling
bead has landed, strengthen the check to verify the recorded sha is an ancestor
of HEAD (`git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> HEAD`). Where it has not, note the
limitation in the check's own text rather than implying more than it proves.

Consider whether this belongs in a small script alongside the other three
bundled scripts. Argument for: it is two commands with an ordering and a
failure vocabulary, which is the stated reason the other three exist, and it
runs on every bead. Argument against: it is genuinely two lines. Decide, and
say which in the retro; if scripted, publish its usage line in the interface
table.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Phase 3 has an acceptance-check step that runs after each outcome and before the bead enters the run table
- [ ] The check tests for a non-empty retro file and a committed event in the progress ledger
- [ ] A failing check yields status 'ceremony-incomplete', not 'closed'
- [ ] The remedy is stated: reconstruct the retro and backfill events; do not reopen the bead or amend the commit
- [ ] The check is stated to apply per bead within batch dispatch modes, not once per batch
- [ ] The Phase 4 report lists every bead whose anchor was missing or reconstructed, and an aggregated retro says which beads contributed nothing
- [ ] The check's text states what it does not prove about sha reachability, or verifies ancestry where the sha-drift fix has landed
- [ ] The script-or-inline decision is made and recorded, and any script's usage line is published in the interface table
notes:
## Artifact renamed, 2026-08-10

The per-bead artifact is now `{ID}.handoff.md`, not `{ID}.retro.md` — it
carries the paths to stage and any close caveat, and no findings. The check
becomes:

    test -s "$RUN_DIR/$ID.handoff.md" &&
      grep -q '"phase":"committed"' "$RUN_DIR/$ID.progress.jsonl"

Coordinate with the sibling bead that performs the rename — whichever lands
second must not reintroduce the old name. The failure status stays
`ceremony-incomplete`, and the remedy still reconstructs the missing artifact
rather than reopening the bead or amending the commit.

Note the acceptance check is now the ONLY enforcement that the handoff file
exists: `bb-close-bead.sh` used to refuse to run without it, and that guard is
being removed with the body-file argument.

metadata.tier_reason: Two-command check with a defined failure vocabulary and a Phase 4 consequence; one open call (script or inline) with the trade stated.

title: recovery.md: add the orchestrator-death entry procedure, and bound what the progress ledger proves
description:
`references/recovery.md` covers subagent death and nothing else. Its scope line
(`:3`) is "how it recovers when a [subagent dies]" and its procedure section is
headed `## Subagent crash / mid-step timeout recovery` (`:19`). Every step
presumes a live orchestrator that knows the run.

**The orchestrator is what died.** Run `1786121603-ri` closed 8 beads across 7
subagents in ~1h40m, was killed mid-batch by a user interrupt at 18:33:08, and
sat dead for 2h16m. Two kill notifications were enqueued at 18:33:08.862 and
.863 and never dequeued — every other notification in that transcript shows an
enqueue followed ~50ms later by a dequeue. The same interrupt stopped the
orchestrator, so the mechanism that would have reported the death died with it.
The UI showed the task running.

Recovery was then reconstructed by hand over ~30 minutes from git mtimes, `bd`,
and raw session transcripts — while the run directory held `dispatch.md`,
`decisions.md`, seven `.retro.md` anchors (4.3–17.5 KB each) and eight
`.progress.jsonl` files. `agent-plugins-9kb.5.progress.jsonl` contained exactly
the conclusion the orchestrator derived forensically:

```
{"bead":"agent-plugins-9kb.5","phase":"claimed"}
{"bead":"agent-plugins-9kb.5","phase":"implementing"}
```

The recovering agent invented a procedure, and the one it invented was wrong in
a way it had to correct mid-run: it keyed liveness on
`bd list --status in_progress`, which returns empty while an unclaimed agent is
actively working — observed `open` while twelve files were being edited.

**And the ledger it would have read is not authoritative.**
`recovery.md:40-55` presents the event sequence as the status surface without
bounding its authority. `9kb.5`'s trail ends at `implementing` with mtime 18:29
while the bead was committed at 21:06 (`bb7ecc3`), four beads later. A heartbeat
in that run read a trail ending at `implementing` as "positive proof of a live
agent at a known phase". It was proof of nothing except that nothing had been
appended.

Both gaps live in one file, so they are one bead.
design:
Two additions to `references/recovery.md`.

## 1. New section: `## Orchestrator crash / context loss — resuming a run`

Ordered entry procedure:

> 1. **Find the run.** `bd show <epic-id>` for the RUN_DIR pointer, or
>    `ls -l "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/claude/bead-bonanza/current"`. WHEN neither exists
>    the run predates the pointer: reconstruct from `git log` and
>    `bd list --status all`, and say so in the report.
> 2. **Read `dispatch.md`.** It carries the mandate, the enumerated bead list,
>    the standing authorization, the wave table, the gate profile and the
>    environmental ledger. **This is the plan — do not re-derive it, and do not
>    re-run the filter that produced it.** Read `## Amendments` too; the plan
>    may have moved.
> 3. **Establish liveness — git is primary, the tracker is corroboration.** A
>    bead may be worked without being claimed, so `bd list --status in_progress`
>    can be empty during live work. Use the newest dirty-file mtime:
>    newest < ~5 min -> an agent is alive; do not dispatch, do not commit its
>    files. > ~30 min -> orphaned work from a killed child; recover it. No dirty
>    files -> idle.
> 4. **Classify each in-scope bead** by its `<bead>.progress.jsonl` tail, then
>    corroborate per the authority rule below: absent -> may never have started;
>    `claimed`/`implementing` -> may have died mid-work; `gates-passed`/
>    `retro-written` -> finish the close from `<bead>.retro.md`; `committed` ->
>    verify the sha is an ancestor of HEAD.
> 5. **Verify every claim against `bd` and `git` yourself.** A completion
>    notification is not proof; one was lost entirely in this run.

**The mtime command must be portable.** The observed one-liner uses
`stat -c '%Y %n'`, which is GNU-only and fails on macOS. Provide a probed
wrapper (`stat -c` / `stat -f '%m %N'`) or use `find`/`ls -t`, and say which. A
recovery procedure that fails on the recovering agent's platform is not a
procedure. Reuse the wrapper the pre-flight script establishes rather than
writing a second one.

## 2. New rule directly under the event schema: the ledger is a hint

> **The ledger is a hint, never the authority.** It is written by the agent
> doing the work, so it stops the instant that agent stops. Therefore:
>
> - A trail ending before `committed` does **not** mean the bead is unfinished —
>   only that nothing was appended after that point.
> - An absent progress file does **not** mean no agent ran.
> - A file's mtime bounds the last *write*, not the agent's liveness.
>
> Resolve any status question in this order, stopping at the first answer:
> `bd show <id>`, then `git log --oneline --grep=<id>`, then the ledger. Name
> which one you used. Never report a ledger fact you have not just read from
> disk, and never from a backup copy while the live directory exists.

Do not add timestamps to progress events — `recovery.md:58` records a deliberate
decision against them, and the cross-check above resolves the question without
one.

## Wiring

`SKILL.md`'s Reference-files table currently loads `recovery.md` WHEN "a
subagent crashed, timed out, or is running past 5 minutes". Widen that condition
to include resuming a run whose state you do not hold — otherwise the new
section is only found by an agent that already knows to look for it.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] references/recovery.md has an 'Orchestrator crash / context loss — resuming a run' section with the five ordered steps
- [ ] Step 2 forbids re-deriving the plan or re-running the filter, and requires reading the Amendments section
- [ ] Step 3 states that git dirty-file mtime is primary and bd claim status is not a liveness signal, with the <5min / >30min / no-dirty-files thresholds
- [ ] The mtime command works on macOS and Linux via a probed wrapper, and the retro records it running on both
- [ ] A 'the ledger is a hint, never the authority' rule sits directly under the event schema, with the three negative statements and the bd -> git log -> ledger resolution order
- [ ] No timestamps were added to progress events
- [ ] SKILL.md's Reference-files table load condition for recovery.md covers resuming a run whose state the orchestrator does not hold

metadata.tier_reason: Authors a procedure that runs when everything else has failed, keyed on a liveness signal that is counter-intuitive and platform-dependent. Getting the ranking wrong reproduces the observed 2h16m stall.

title: Bucket beads on C4 blast radius, not prose-scanned file paths, and treat impacts-intersects-changes as a sequencing constraint
description:
`bead-bonanza` buckets beads for parallel and batched dispatch by guessing at
file overlap from prose, while the signal it needs is already computed,
declared and queryable — and it never reads it.

`SKILL.md:404-405`:

> Find file overlap by scanning each bead's description for fixture names +
> source paths, then bucketing by overlap.

Meanwhile `groom-beads` writes C4 blast radius into bead metadata for exactly
this purpose. `plugin/skills/groom-beads/SKILL.md:236-266`:

```
bd update <id> --metadata '{"tier":"standard",...,
  "c4_changes":["auth-service"],"c4_impacts":["web-spa","billing-service"],
  "c4_docs":["docs/c4/auth-service/component.md"]}'
```

> This pays off three ways: **wave isolation** (two beads that both *change*
> `auth-service` are a collision even when both are `bd ready` —
> dependency-free != safe-to-parallelize) ...

and `groom-beads/SKILL.md:314-322` offers a **wave preview**, grouping ready
beads under "dependencies **and** no two beads sharing a `c4_changes` component
in the same wave", explicitly "for the orchestrator to accept or ignore" and
"hands it the C4-collision insight for free".

Measured 2026-08-10:

```
$ grep -rn "c4\|C4" plugin/skills/bead-bonanza/
```
returns hits only in the vendored `references/shared/work-order-definition-of-ready.md`
(a generated copy the skill does not act on) and one passing mention of "C4
blast radius" inside the grooming subagent prompt. **Phase 2.5 reads no C4
field.** The producer computes the signal, names the orchestrator as its
consumer, and the consumer re-derives a worse version from prose.

Two classes of collision the current heuristic cannot see:

1. **Same component, disjoint files.** Two beads that both change a component's
   behaviour through different files read as `isolated` and get parallelized.
2. **Producer and consumer of a contract.** Bead A changes a component that
   bead B's component depends on — `A.c4_changes` intersects `B.c4_impacts`.
   Zero file overlap, and B must be sequenced after A. Today they batch or
   parallelize happily.

Note for the implementer: this repository has **no C4 docs** (`docs/` contains
only `session-bootstrap.md`), so its own beads carry no `c4_*` metadata. The
fallback path is therefore the one exercised here, and the C4 path must be
verified against a fixture rather than against this repo's live beads.
design:
Rewrite Phase 2.5's "Classify each bead" overlap rule. Three layers, in
precedence order.

**1. C4 metadata is the primary signal where it exists.**

```bash
bd list --status open --json | jq -r '.[] | select(.id=="<id>") | .metadata'
```

- Two beads sharing any `c4_changes` component are `shared-surface`, whatever
  their file paths say. They may batch (one subagent, sequential, one commit
  each); they SHALL NOT go in the same worktree-parallel wave.
- Bead B whose `c4_impacts` intersects bead A's `c4_changes` is a **consumer of
  a contract A is changing**. That is a *sequencing* constraint, not a batching
  one: order B after A in the same bucket, or wire a real `blocks` edge when the
  ordering must survive the run. Distinguish this in the plan's Reason column —
  "consumes auth-service, changed by <id>" reads very differently from "same
  fixture cluster".
- Beads with disjoint `c4_changes` and no impact intersection are `isolated`
  with respect to architecture; they may still collide on files, so layer 2
  still runs.

**2. File-path overlap is the fallback and the corroborator.** Keep the existing
prose scan for repos with no C4 docs, and run it alongside C4 where both exist.
A conflict between the two signals — disjoint components, overlapping files — is
information: it usually means the C4 tagging is wrong or a bead's scope is wider
than its tags say. Treat the union as the collision set and note the discrepancy
in the plan; do not silently prefer one.

**3. Consume the wave preview.** WHEN the grooming subagent returns a wave
preview (`groom-beads` produces one by default), take it as the starting
partition rather than re-deriving it, and record in the dispatch plan whether it
was accepted or overridden and why. The orchestrator stays the source of truth
on packing — the preview is an input, not an instruction. Add this to the
grooming subagent prompt's return contract in `references/subagent-prompts.md`
so the preview actually comes back: the template's current return format is one
line per bead and has no slot for it.

**4. Say what happens with no C4 docs.** One sentence: where the repo has no C4
documentation, grooming skips the tagging, `c4_*` is absent, and file-overlap
scanning is the whole signal. Do not treat absent metadata as "no collisions".

## Verification

This repo has no C4 docs, so build a fixture: two or three beads with
hand-written `c4_changes`/`c4_impacts` metadata in a scratch state, and confirm
the bucketing rule classifies (a) shared-component/disjoint-file as
shared-surface, (b) impacts-intersects-changes as a sequencing constraint, and
(c) fully disjoint as isolated. Record the observed classifications in the retro
— per the ledger convention, a rule asserted without a run is not evidence.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Phase 2.5 reads c4_changes and c4_impacts from bead metadata as the primary overlap signal
- [ ] Two beads sharing a c4_changes component are classified shared-surface regardless of file paths, and are never placed in the same worktree-parallel wave
- [ ] An impacts-intersects-changes pair is treated as a sequencing constraint and is distinguishable from a co-edit collision in the plan's Reason column
- [ ] File-path scanning is retained as fallback and corroborator, with the union taken as the collision set and any discrepancy noted in the plan
- [ ] The grooming subagent prompt's return contract includes the wave preview, and the skill records whether the preview was accepted or overridden
- [ ] SKILL.md states what happens when the repo has no C4 docs, and that absent metadata does not mean no collisions
- [ ] The three classification cases were exercised against a metadata fixture and the observed results are recorded in the retro

metadata.tier_reason: New bucketing logic spanning two skills' contracts, a three-way precedence rule, and a fixture to verify it because this repo has no C4 docs to test against.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: Fixture verification (scratch bd project under /tmp, four beads, not committed): A(changes auth-service, impacts billing-service), B(changes auth-service), C(changes web-spa, impacts auth-service), D(changes reporting-service). Observed: co-edit A+B on auth-service with zero file overlap; sequencing C after A and C after B (consumes auth-service); D isolated. The documented jq ran clean against this repo's untagged beads too — empty output, exit 0, no error from the missing keys.

comments.text: retro: Settled an implicit decision the bead left open — where the accepted/overridden wave-preview record lives. Put it in the dispatch plan's run manifest as a 'Wave preview' row (accepted | overridden — why | none (no C4 docs) | not returned) rather than in the Amendments log, so recovery reads it without replaying the log.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: A choice a diff-reader would not see as one: a sequencing constraint deliberately does NOT get its own bead class. The three classes stay trivial/isolated/shared-surface, and an impacts-intersects-changes pair is expressed as wave ordering plus a Reason-column phrase — so a consumer bead can still read 'isolated' while running in a later wave. The alternative (a fourth class) was tried first and abandoned: it would have made every consumer look like a co-edit collision in the bucket column, which is exactly the conflation this bead exists to remove.
